analysis.title: US Economic Weekly: Revisions, risks, and rate hikes
key_insights: BEA revised inflation data lower after methodological changes to portfolio management and investment advice, computer and software accessories, and legal services. The revisions were somewhat larger than BofA anticipated.

BofA still estimates underlying inflation at 2.5% y/y, with little evidence the trend improved over the past 12 months. Risks remain tilted to the upside from AI demand, energy, the labor market and strong consumer growth.
BofA expects the Fed to take a risk management approach and tighten policy at its remaining two meetings this year, even if inflation is softer after the revisions.
2Q GDP growth was revised up by 70bp to 2.2% in the final estimate. 1Q GDP was raised by 40bp to 2.5% and annual growth in 2024/25 was revised higher.
BofA raised its 2026 GDP forecast by 20bp to 2.3% Q4/Q4. It reads firmer momentum as pointing to stronger productivity growth and a higher neutral rate.

The week ahead is light on data. The FOMC minutes (Wed) are the focus, with final S&P Global services PMI and ISM services Mon, trade data Tue, claims Thu and consumer sentiment Fri. Williams and Logan speak Tue, Musalem Thu.
The minutes should show whether the committee sees the September hike as a midcycle adjustment or the start of a full hiking cycle. The vote was unanimous.

Hyperscaler capex is projected to rise roughly 90% y/y this year and a further 36% next year. BofA expects limited direct inflation impact because electrical equipment, computers and electronics are a small share of consumption.

Iran and Russia-Ukraine conflicts have caused persistent energy and refined product shortages, lifting headline inflation via gasoline and core via airfares. Transportation services are about 0.7% of consumption and petroleum and coal products 1.2%, so the pass-through is limited.

Aggregate labor market is not a major inflation source: vacancy-to-unemployment ratio is near 1.0, quits are well below 2021-23 highs and wage growth is moderating. Data center and AI-linked industries have faster wage growth than the private sector.
BofA's base case is a divided Congress after the midterms, with very little chance of policy changes large enough to alter the growth, earnings or AI investment backdrop over the next two years.

BofA is more bullish on the US consumer. Risks have shifted modestly to the upside, the K-shaped consumer story looks stale and lower-income spending growth is rebounding. Gas prices, credit and equity market risks remain.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Revised down by 35bp by the BEA methodology change. BofA says this does not change the underlying inflation view.
Printed at the same 3.0% y/y as revised July.
BofA's own estimate, with little evidence of improvement over 12 months. It supports a further Fed tightening.
Revised up by 70bp, pointing to firmer momentum.
Marked up by 20bp after the revisions.
A sizeable demand shock with limited direct inflation pass-through absent supply constraints.
The aggregate labor market is not a significant source of inflation pressure.

risk_factors: Inflation risks tilted to the upside from AI-related investment, higher energy prices, pockets of labor market tightness and resilient consumer demand.
Higher diesel and fuel costs could gradually feed into broader consumer prices via transportation and logistics.
Strong profit growth and continued investment could reignite labor demand and reintroduce wage-price dynamics.
Continued strength of consumer demand risks overheating the economy.
Gas prices, credit and equity market risks remain for the consumer.
charts_described: Exhibit 3 plots a diffusion index of Fed participants' risk weightings on core PCE, with the FOMC nearly unanimous that risks skew to the upside.

Exhibit 4 shows shares of total consumption for specific inputs in 2024: transportation costs 0.69%, petroleum and coal products 1.22%, electrical equipment 0.43%, computer and electronic products 0.02%.
geopolitical: Conflicts involving Iran and Russia-Ukraine have contributed to persistent shortages in energy and refined petroleum products.
US midterms: BofA's base case is a divided Congress.

tension_points.bull_case: Revisions lowered the level of core PCE by 35bp in July, a dovish read that could argue against further tightening.
tension_points.bear_case: Underlying inflation is still 2.5% and risks skew to the upside from AI demand, energy, labor and consumer strength, so BofA expects the Fed to tighten at its remaining two meetings.

theme_stances.key_argument: Underlying inflation is unchanged at 2.5% with upside risks, so the Fed takes a risk management approach and tightens further.
theme_stances.evidence: the Fed will take a risk management approach and tighten policy

theme_stances.key_argument: Lower-income spending growth is rebounding and labor market broadening and healthy balance sheets support spending.
theme_stances.evidence: The K-shaped consumer story is looking stale
